# Nordic mammals — provenance report

**Deck:** [`decks/nordic-mammals.ttl`](../decks/nordic-mammals.ttl) · **Cards:** 63 · **Licence:** [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) · **Compiled by:** Anton Wiklund · **Created:** 2026-10-04

63 wild mammals of Sweden and the Nordic countries: large predators, deer, rodents, shrews, bats, seals, whales and dolphins. Front: the English and the Swedish name; back: the scientific name. Scientific and English names follow the Mammal Diversity Database (v2.5; English names in British spelling), Swedish names Dyntaxa (SLU Artdatabanken). Data from Wikidata, Dyntaxa and the Mammal Diversity Database, checked against Swedish Wikipedia.

## Licensing

The deck is released under CC BY 4.0 because two of its content sources are published under CC BY 4.0: the Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 (Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.21654811) and GRIIS - Sweden (GBIF, 10.15468/i57bff). The English names on the cards follow MDD (a number of them, such as 'western red deer' or 'common whiskered myotis', are in no CC0 source in that form), and MDD is the taxonomic authority behind the scientific names; GRIIS is the second source for the 'non-native in Sweden' notes. Both are attributed in the deck (prov:wasDerivedFrom, with title, creator and licence) and in this report. The other content sources are CC0: Wikidata (structured data) for the taxon names and the labels, and Dyntaxa (SLU Artdatabanken, published on GBIF under CC0 1.0) for every Swedish name and the Swedish status of each species; CC0 material may be included in a CC BY deck. Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) and an SVT news article (all rights reserved) were used for verification only: they confirmed that each Swedish name denotes the species and the background of the non-native species; nothing in the cards rests on them alone, no text, list or selection was taken from them, and the short phrases quoted in the evidence are citations. The selection of species is the authoring agent's own.

## Method

1. Scope and authority. The library editor asked for about 60 wild mammals of Sweden and the Nordic countries, land and marine, with the common name (English and Swedish) on the front and the scientific name on the back, using one stated taxonomic authority consistently. The Mammal Diversity Database (MDD) of the American Society of Mammalogists was chosen as the single authority for scientific and English names: its current release, v2.5 of 28 July 2026, was confirmed on its home page and its Zenodo record on 2026-10-04. Swedish names follow Dyntaxa, the Swedish taxonomic database of SLU Artdatabanken, as published under CC0 on GBIF (dataset publication date 2026-09-29).
2. Candidate list. The authoring agent wrote down 79 candidate species from general knowledge of the Nordic mammal fauna (the big four predators and other carnivores, seals, deer and other ungulates, whales and dolphins, hares, rodents, hedgehog, mole, shrews and bats), using the names it expected MDD to use, plus 10 older or alternative names (for example Myodes glareolus, Eptesicus nilssonii, Neovison vison, Phoca hispida, Alopex lagopus) to see how the sources treat them. One candidate, Microtus oeconomus, is not an MDD v2.5 name (MDD: Alexandromys oeconomus), so the second pass used Alexandromys oeconomus. No published list was copied.
3. Wikidata (content source). One SPARQL query (the first query below) fetched, for every candidate and alternative name, the items with that taxon name (P225), their rank (P105), English and Swedish labels and aliases, and Dyntaxa id (P1939). A second query (the second below) did the same for the final MDD names and Dyntaxa's accepted names.
4. Dyntaxa (content source). Each name was looked up in the Dyntaxa checklist on GBIF (species search restricted to the dataset, exact canonical name), and for each matching record its vernacular names (with GBIF's 'preferred' flag, which marks Dyntaxa's recommended Swedish name), synonyms and Swedish distribution record (status, establishment means, threat status) were fetched. In a second pass the records were fetched under Dyntaxa's own accepted names where they differ from MDD's (Myodes glareolus for Clethrionomys glareolus, Neovison vison for Neogale vison).
5. MDD (content source and authority). The release file MDD_v2.5_6904species.csv was downloaded from the Zenodo record of v2.5, and each candidate's row was looked up by sciName, recording id, authority, mainCommonName, otherCommonNames, originalNameCombination, taxonomyNotes and countryDistribution.
6. Selection. The candidates were filtered by the criteria in the selection section and cut by editorial judgement to the most familiar species; exclusions and reasons are listed there.
7. Card text. Back: the MDD v2.5 scientific name, tagged as Latin; it is also the taxon name (P225) of a Wikidata item, and Dyntaxa's accepted name for all but two cards (bank vole and American mink, where Dyntaxa lists the MDD name as a synonym). English front: MDD's main English name, written in British spelling (grey, harbour, particoloured) and in lower case except proper nouns and words derived from them (Eurasian, European, Arctic, Norway, West European, Daubenton's, Natterer's, Nathusius's, American); for three species MDD's main name is not the usual European name and another of MDD's English names is used: stoat (main name 'Beringian Ermine'), reindeer ('Caribou') and wild boar ('Eurasian Wild Pig'). A script (ambiguity.py, last query) compared each English front, ignoring letter case and British/American spelling, with every main and other English name of all 6,904 MDD species: each front is a name of its own species only. Swedish front: Dyntaxa's preferred Swedish vernacular name, exactly as Dyntaxa writes it, except for the reindeer, whose preferred Dyntaxa name 'vildren' means wild reindeer; the card uses Dyntaxa's other name 'ren', which is also the Wikidata Swedish label and the Swedish Wikipedia article. No Swedish text was translated by the agent except the notes.
8. Notes. Back notes give former scientific names (from Dyntaxa synonyms, MDD's taxonomic notes and original combinations, and Wikidata items or aliases), where Dyntaxa's name differs from MDD's, common alternative English or Swedish names (from MDD's other names, Dyntaxa's other Swedish names and Wikidata aliases; a Swedish note gives an alternative English name whenever the English note does), the species that are not native to Sweden (see the next paragraph), and two short clarifications: the moose's English name 'elk' (an MDD other name of both Alces alces and Cervus canadensis; Wikidata's Swedish label of Cervus canadensis is 'vapiti') and the status of wild reindeer (Dyntaxa: regionally extinct in Sweden; MDD: occurs in Norway and Finland). Alternative Swedish names are given as 'Swedish also …' / 'Kallas också …': Dyntaxa lists them as other (non-preferred) names but does not say whether they are older names, so the notes do not call them earlier names. The Swedish notes were written by the authoring agent.
9. Non-native species (added in review round 1, narrowed in round 4). The note 'Non-native in Sweden.' / 'Främmande art i Sverige.' marks the five species that two open content sources both list as introduced in Sweden: Dyntaxa's Swedish distribution record (establishment means INTRODUCED) and the Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species (GRIIS) - Sweden on GBIF (CC BY 4.0; establishment means INTRODUCED), fetched with the GBIF species search restricted to that dataset and each record's distributions. These are the American mink, common raccoon dog, European hare, European rabbit and common muskrat. The notes say only that the species is non-native, not how it arrived: for the muskrat and the raccoon dog, sources differ on or describe spread from Finland rather than a release in Sweden. GRIIS also lists the common fallow deer, red deer, wild boar, brown rat and house mouse as introduced, but Dyntaxa lists the fallow deer, red deer, brown rat and house mouse as NATIVE and gives no establishment means for the wild boar (its record https://api.gbif.org/v1/species/159940004/distributions has only SE, PRESENT) (Swedish Wikipedia, as verification, says fallow deer were probably brought to Sweden in the second half of the 16th century and red deer came about 10,000 years ago). A review in round 4 pointed out that SLU Artdatabanken, which publishes Dyntaxa, treats species that people brought in and that became established before 1800 as part of the Swedish fauna, and that 'främmande art' is its term for later arrivals; the agent saw this only in a search snippet, so it is not stated on any card. Because the status of these long-established populations depends on the convention used and the two content sources do not both say INTRODUCED, those five cards carry no such note.
10. Cross-check with Swedish Wikipedia (verification). For every Swedish front the Swedish Wikipedia API was asked for the article the name leads to (following redirects) and the first sentences of its introduction. For 57 names the article was the species; 'lo', 'iller', 'älg', 'tumlare', 'bäver' and 'vildkanin' led to a disambiguation page, the genus, the family or a hatnote, and the species articles Lodjur, Iller, Europeisk älg, Vanlig tumlare, Europeisk bäver and Europeisk kanin were fetched instead. Every article's introduction gives the card's Swedish name (or, for 'mindre skogsmus', 'vikval', 'knölval' and 'fransfladdermus', its definite form) for the card's species; three give an older scientific name (Clethrionomys rufocanus, Microtus oeconomus, Eptesicus serotinus with the synonym Cnephaeus serotinus) and one treats the moose as two species, all recorded under quality control.
11. Machine checks. Each card has a Wikidata check of the taxon name (P225) of the item with the MDD name, and checks of its English and Swedish fronts as a label or alias wherever Wikidata has that text in exactly the card's letter case (on the item with the MDD name, or for five species whose Wikidata item under the MDD name has no labels, on the item under the older name). The builder runs them against live Wikidata on every build. Where Wikidata links the item with the MDD name to the labelled item by 'taxon synonym' (P1420) — the bank vole (Q50407592 → Q216580) and the root vole (Q125399268 → Q703702) — that link is checked too, so the label check and the taxon-name check are tied to one species; for the grey red-backed vole, northern serotine and Eurasian serotine Wikidata has no direct statement between the two items (query below) and the link rests on Dyntaxa's and MDD's synonym lists.
12. Process. The research, drafting and cross-checking were done by AI agents (Claude, Anthropic) at Anton Wiklund's direction, with independent AI reviewers who cross-checked the cards and documentation (review rounds 1–5 below) and machine checks by the deck builder and the app's validators. The cards have not yet been reviewed by a human subject expert (a mammalogist).

## Selection

The deck has 63 wild mammal species of Sweden and the Nordic countries: 14 carnivores (including the big four: brown bear, grey wolf, Eurasian lynx and wolverine), 3 seals, 6 deer and other ungulates, 5 whales, dolphins and porpoises, 3 hares and rabbits, 16 rodents, 5 hedgehogs, moles and shrews, and 11 bats. Inclusion criteria: (1) a species in MDD v2.5; (2) an accepted Dyntaxa taxon (under the MDD name or a name Dyntaxa lists the MDD name as a synonym of) with a preferred Swedish vernacular name; (3) regularly occurring in the Nordic countries: Dyntaxa's Swedish distribution status PRESENT (native or introduced and established), or, for the reindeer and four cetaceans that Dyntaxa lists as IRREGULAR in Sweden (common minke whale, common killer whale, humpback whale, white-beaked dolphin), Norway among MDD's countries for the species; (4) a Wikidata item with the MDD name as taxon name; (5) an English name that is unambiguous among all MDD species. Introduced species are included when Dyntaxa lists them as present (American mink, common raccoon dog, European hare, European rabbit, common muskrat). Dyntaxa's status PRESENT is out of date for the common raccoon dog: Svenska Jägareförbundet declared it functionally eradicated as a breeding species in Sweden in early 2025, though single animals still cross from Finland (SVT, 7 January 2025; Swedish Wikipedia, both verification). The card is kept because the species is established in Finland, a Nordic country (Swedish Wikipedia: about 150,000 shot there a year). Familiarity to a Nordic beginner decided the final cut. Left out after research: Clethrionomys rutilus (northern red-backed vole, rödsork), Myotis brandtii (Brandt's myotis, tajgafladdermus; hard to tell from the whiskered myotis), Barbastella barbastellus (barbastell), Micromys minutus (dvärgmus), Sorex caecutiens (lappnäbbmus) and Sorex minutissimus (mindre dvärgnäbbmus), only to keep the deck near the requested size; Pagophilus groenlandicus (grönlandssäl), Erignathus barbatus (storsäl) and Odocoileus virginianus (vitsvanshjort): Dyntaxa status in Sweden IRREGULAR; Balaenoptera physalus, Physeter macrocephalus, Globicephala melas and Tursiops truncatus: irregular in Sweden and less often met than the whales kept; Ovibos moschatus (myskoxe): present in Sweden only as a small introduced herd; Pteromys volans (Siberian flying squirrel) and Cystophora cristata (hooded seal): no Dyntaxa record found. Taxonomy: names follow MDD v2.5 throughout, also where Dyntaxa differs (Clethrionomys glareolus, Dyntaxa Myodes glareolus; Neogale vison, Dyntaxa Neovison vison), with Dyntaxa's name in a back note. MDD treats the moose of Eurasia and North America as one species (Alces alces) and keeps the reindeer as one species (Rangifer tarandus, not following the six-species split proposed in 2022); MDD v2.5 treats the Saimaa ringed seal of Finland as a species of its own (Pusa saimensis), so the ringed seal card means Pusa hispida, which includes the Baltic ringed seal. Subspecies are not included.

## Queries

**Candidate species and alternative names: Wikidata item, rank, English and Swedish labels and aliases, Dyntaxa id (POST to https://query.wikidata.org/sparql, format json; saved as wikidata-candidates.json)** (Wikidata)

```
SELECT ?name ?item ?rank ?en ?sv (GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT ?enAlt; separator="|") AS ?enAlts) (GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT ?svAlt; separator="|") AS ?svAlts) (GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT ?dyntaxa; separator="|") AS ?dyn) WHERE {

  ?item wdt:P225 ?name ; wdt:P105 ?rank .

  OPTIONAL { ?item wdt:P1939 ?dyntaxa }
} GROUP BY ?name ?item ?rank ?en ?sv
```

**Ambiguity check of each English front against every MDD v2.5 species. Algorithm: read MDD_v2.5_6904species.csv; for every row take mainCommonName and each '|'-separated entry of otherCommonNames; normalise a name by lower-casing it, replacing 'grey' by 'gray', 'harbour' by 'harbor' and 'coloured' by 'colored', and then deleting every character other than a–z (so spaces, hyphens and apostrophes are ignored); index the normalised names by species. A front passes when its normalised form is a name of the card's species and of no other species. The script, verbatim:** (Mammal Diversity Database, version 2.5)

```
import csv, re
from pathlib import Path
from species import SPECIES  # the cards: (id, sciName, English front, Swedish front)
DIR = Path(__file__).parent

def norm(s):
    s = s.lower().replace("grey", "gray").replace("harbour", "harbor").replace("coloured", "colored")
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z]", "", s)

index = {}
for r in csv.DictReader(open(DIR / "MDD_v2.5_6904species.csv", encoding="utf-8")):
    names = [r["mainCommonName"]] + [x for x in r["otherCommonNames"].split("|") if x]
    for i, n in enumerate(names):
        index.setdefault(norm(n), []).append((r["sciName"].replace("_", " "), "main" if i == 0 else "other"))
for cid, sci, en, sv in SPECIES:
    hits = index.get(norm(en), [])
    mine = [h for h in hits if h[0] == sci]
    others = [h for h in hits if h[0] != sci]
    flag = "OK " if mine and not others else "?? "
    print(flag, cid, en, "->", mine, "OTHERS:" if others else "", others)
```

## Quality control

6 rounds, 35 findings: 27 fixed, 1 rejected after checking, 7 needing no change. Every card's Wikidata checks (144 in all) are re-run against live Wikidata by `scripts/authored_decks.py check` before every build.

### Round 0: Sources and machine checks: every card's scientific, English and Swedish names compared across MDD v2.5, Dyntaxa (GBIF), Wikidata and Swedish Wikipedia; English names checked for ambiguity against all MDD species. (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — authoring agent, machine checks · **Scope:** All 63 cards and the candidates left out.

All 63 scientific names are MDD v2.5 names and the taxon name (P225) of a Wikidata item (checked by the builder); 61 are Dyntaxa's accepted name and the other two are Dyntaxa synonyms of its accepted name. All Swedish fronts are Dyntaxa's preferred name (the reindeer: Dyntaxa's other name 'ren') and lead to the species on Swedish Wikipedia. Every English front is an MDD name of its species and of no other MDD species. ### Round 1: Factual accuracy (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — independent Factual accuracy reviewer · **Scope:** All 63 cards, re-checked against the Dyntaxa checklist on GBIF (2026-09-29), the MDD v2.5 species file and live Wikidata; the round 0 fixes.

No name errors. The reviewer found the raccoon dog's 'Introduced to Sweden' note wrong and out of date, the muskrat's disputed, and the fallow deer's missing note misleading; all three were verified and the introduced-species notes were rewritten as 'Non-native in Sweden' backed by Dyntaxa and a second open source (GRIIS - Sweden, CC BY 4.0). Taxon-synonym checks now tie two of the split Wikidata items together.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| raccoon-dog | 'Introduced to Sweden' is wrong and out of date: the raccoon dog spread to Sweden from Finland, and Svenska Jägareförbundet declared it eradicated as a breeding species in Sweden in 2025; Dyntaxa's status PRESENT lags behind. | Verified today on Swedish Wikipedia (Mårdhund) and SVT (7 January 2025: 'Idag är mårdhunden funktionellt utrotad i Sverige'). The note now says only what two open content sources support, 'Non-native in Sweden.' / 'Främmande art i Sverige.' (Dyntaxa and GRIIS - Sweden: INTRODUCED). The suggested wording about spread from Finland and eradication in 2025 rests only on verification sources (Swedish Wikipedia, CC BY-SA; SVT, all rights reserved), so it is not put on the card but recorded in the selection (Dyntaxa's PRESENT is out of date; the card is kept because the species is established in Finland) and in the card's evidence, with SVT added as a verification source. | fixed |
| muskrat | 'Introduced to Sweden' claims a deliberate introduction, which sources dispute (a 1944 release in the Torne valley versus spontaneous spread from Finland around 1950). | Verified on Swedish Wikipedia (Bisam). The note is now 'Non-native in Sweden.' / 'Främmande art i Sverige.', which Dyntaxa and GRIIS - Sweden both support and which says nothing about how it arrived. The reviewer's alternative ('spread to Sweden from about 1950') is itself one side of the dispute and was not used. | fixed |
| fallow-deer | The fallow deer was brought to Sweden by people (16th century) but, unlike the other introduced species, has no note, because Dyntaxa lists it as NATIVE. | Verified: GRIIS - Sweden lists Dama dama as INTRODUCED and Swedish Wikipedia says it was probably brought in during the second half of the 16th century; Dyntaxa says NATIVE (with a red-list category, LEAST_CONCERN). The card now has the same note as the other non-native species, 'Non-native in Sweden.' / 'Främmande art i Sverige.', with the discrepancy in the evidence and the method. The century is not on the card, as it rests on Swedish Wikipedia alone. GRIIS also lists red deer, wild boar, brown rat and house mouse as introduced; Dyntaxa lists them as native and they get no note (explained in the method). | fixed |
| bank-vole | On cards whose species is split over two Wikidata items, the label check and the taxon-name check are on different items and do not tie the front to the back (also grey-red-backed-vole, root-vole, northern-bat, serotine). | A SPARQL query for direct statements between the paired items found 'taxon synonym' (P1420) from Q50407592 to Q216580 (bank vole) and from Q125399268 to Q703702 (root vole); both are now checked. For grey-red-backed-vole (Q125628803/Q844638), northern-bat (Q125880762/Q300941) and serotine (Q125881069/Q214869) Wikidata has no statement linking the items, so no such check is possible; the tie rests on Dyntaxa's synonyms and MDD's taxonomic notes, recorded in each card's evidence. Checking P225 'Myodes glareolus' on Q216580 would not tie the two items and was not added. | fixed |

### Round 3: Licensing, attribution and documentation (2026-10-04)
